subject: history
title: Wind of Change in Africa
welcome_lead: From Ghana 1957 to Zimbabwe 1980: African decolonisation in a generation.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on African decolonisation 1957-80 and Macmillan's Wind of Change speech.
final_note: You have raised flags across a continent.

walkthroughs.h2: Why did decolonisation accelerate after Suez?
walkthroughs.body_html: Suez (1956) showed dependence on the US and undermined imperial prestige. The 1958 French Fifth Republic, the 1960 Belgian withdrawal from Congo, and the 1960 UN Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries created cumulative pressure. Macmillan's January 1960 African tour produced the Wind of Change speech, accepting nationalism as 'a political fact'.

Ghana led in March 1957. Nigeria followed in 1960, Sierra Leone and Tanganyika in 1961. The Mau Mau insurgency (1952-60), brutally suppressed in camps documented by Caroline Elkins, ended formal British rule in Kenya in December 1963 under Kenyatta. Within a decade most of British Africa was independent, though settler regions resisted.

Settler-dominated Southern Rhodesia rejected majority rule. Smith's UDI on 11 November 1965 triggered UN sanctions but not military intervention. Guerrilla war by ZANU and ZAPU forced negotiations at Lancaster House in 1979. Robert Mugabe won the 1980 elections; Zimbabwe gained independence on 18 April 1980, effectively closing British decolonisation in Africa.

mcqs.q: Why did the British Empire end after WWII?
options: Britain voluntarily gave its colonies independence as a moral choice.
The UN forced Britain to grant independence to all colonies in 1945.
Hitler called off the attack to invade the USSR immediately.
Britain was bankrupted by the war, faced rising nationalist movements, and confronted US/Soviet pressure against colonialism in a new world order.
